COPYRIGHT FIRST SALE DOCTRINE — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Jordan T. Reyes · A bronze sculpture titled ‘Pacific Light,’ installed in the plaza in 2015.

PURPOSE OF THIS COPYRIGHT FIRST SALE DOCTRINE INFORMATION SHEET
This Information Sheet describes the federal copyright "first sale" doctrine, codified at 17 U.S.C. § 109 -- the statutory limit on a copyright owner's exclusive distribution right that, once a particular copy or phonorecord of a copyrighted work has been lawfully made and its ownership lawfully transferred, generally allows the person who owns that particular copy to sell, lend, give away, or otherwise dispose of it without needing the copyright owner's further permission. It is prepared by Jordan T. Reyes concerning the following copyrighted work and copy: A bronze sculpture titled ‘Pacific Light,’ installed in the plaza in 2015., in connection with the following transaction or proposed transaction involving that copy: resale of the used textbook through an online marketplace. This Information Sheet describes the statutory text of 17 U.S.C. § 109's core rule and its stated exceptions (for certain rental and lending of phonorecords and computer programs, for public display, and for persons who never acquired ownership of the copy), and two federal appellate decisions applying the doctrine -- one addressing whether the doctrine applies to copies manufactured outside the United States, the other addressing when a distribution described as a "license" is nonetheless a transfer of ownership for purposes of the doctrine. It does not itself determine whether the first sale doctrine applies to, or provides a defense for, any specific copy, transaction, or dispute described above, and it is not a substitute for that case-specific legal determination.

DESCRIPTION OF THE COPY AND THE TRANSACTION AT ISSUE
Copyrighted work and particular copy or phonorecord at issue: A bronze sculpture titled ‘Pacific Light,’ installed in the plaza in 2015. Transaction or proposed transaction involving that copy: resale of the used textbook through an online marketplace. This description is provided by Jordan T. Reyes for reference in connection with the statutory text and case law described in this Information Sheet. Listing a work, copy, and transaction here does not itself establish how that copy was made, how its ownership was transferred (if at all), or whether any statutory exception in 17 U.S.C. § 109 applies to it.

17 U.S.C. § 109(A): THE CORE FIRST SALE RULE
The Copyright Act grants a copyright owner the exclusive right, under 17 U.S.C. § 106(3), to distribute copies or phonorecords of the copyrighted work to the public by sale or other transfer of ownership. A separate provision of the same Act, 17 U.S.C. § 109(a), limits that exclusive distribution right once a particular copy has been lawfully made and its ownership transferred: notwithstanding § 106(3), the owner of a particular copy or phonorecord lawfully made under Title 17 -- or any person that owner authorizes -- is entitled, without needing the copyright owner's authority, to sell or otherwise dispose of possession of that particular copy or phonorecord. This is the provision courts and commentators refer to as the "first sale" doctrine: it limits the copyright owner's distribution right to the first transfer of ownership of a given copy, leaving the owner of that particular copy free to sell, lend, or give it away afterward.

  — 17 U.S.C. § 109(a) (Copyright Act, official U.S. Code text), Limitations on exclusive rights: Effect of transfer of particular copy or phonorecord, subsection (a) (https://uscode.house.gov/view.xhtml?req=granuleid:USC-prelim-title17-section109&num=0&edition=prelim)

17 U.S.C. § 109(B)(1)(A): THE RECORD AND COMPUTER PROGRAM RENTAL EXCEPTION, AND ITS NONPROFIT LIBRARY CARVE-OUT
The first sale doctrine described above does not extend to certain rental, lease, or lending transactions involving sound recordings and computer programs. Under 17 U.S.C. § 109(b)(1)(A), unless authorized by the relevant copyright owner (the owner of copyright in the sound recording, or the owner of copyright in the computer program, and, for a sound recording, the owner of copyright in the musical work embodied in it), neither the owner of a particular phonorecord nor a person in possession of a particular copy of a computer program may, for purposes of direct or indirect commercial advantage, dispose of possession of that phonorecord or computer program by rental, lease, or lending, or by any other act or practice in the nature of rental, lease, or lending. The same subsection then states its own carve-out from that restriction: the restriction does not apply to the rental, lease, or lending of a phonorecord for nonprofit purposes by a nonprofit library or nonprofit educational institution.

17 U.S.C. § 109(C): THE PUBLIC DISPLAY EXCEPTION
A parallel provision applies the same ownership-based logic to the copyright owner's exclusive public display right. Under 17 U.S.C. § 106(5), a copyright owner generally has the exclusive right to display a copyrighted work publicly. Section 109(c) limits that right for a particular lawfully made copy: notwithstanding § 106(5), the owner of a particular copy lawfully made under Title 17 -- or any person that owner authorizes -- is entitled, without the copyright owner's authority, to display that copy publicly, either directly or by projecting no more than one image at a time, to viewers present at the place where the copy is located.

  — 17 U.S.C. § 109(c) (Copyright Act, official U.S. Code text), Limitations on exclusive rights: Effect of transfer of particular copy or phonorecord, subsection (c) (https://uscode.house.gov/view.xhtml?req=granuleid:USC-prelim-title17-section109&num=0&edition=prelim)

17 U.S.C. § 109(D): THE PRIVILEGE BELONGS ONLY TO AN OWNER, NOT A RENTER, LESSEE, OR BORROWER
The first-sale and public-display privileges described above are limited, by the statute's own terms, to a person who owns the particular copy in question. Under 17 U.S.C. § 109(d), the privileges described in § 109(a) (the first sale right to sell or otherwise dispose of a copy) and § 109(c) (the public display right) do not, unless the copyright owner authorizes it, extend to a person who acquired possession of the copy or phonorecord from the copyright owner by rental, lease, loan, or otherwise, without acquiring ownership of it. On the statute's own terms, then, a renter, lessee, bailee, or borrower of a copy does not, by virtue of that possession alone, acquire the § 109(a) or § 109(c) privileges that belong to an owner of the copy.

KIRTSAENG V. JOHN WILEY & SONS, INC.: THE FIRST SALE DOCTRINE APPLIES TO COPIES LAWFULLY MADE ABROAD
The U.S. Supreme Court has described what the first sale doctrine accomplishes in § 106(3) exhaustion terms: once a copy of a copyrighted work has been lawfully sold, or its ownership otherwise lawfully transferred, the "first sale" is said to have "exhausted" the copyright owner's exclusive distribution right under § 106(3) as to that particular copy, leaving the buyer and subsequent owners of that copy free to dispose of it as they wish. In Kirtsaeng v. John Wiley & Sons, Inc., the Court addressed whether this doctrine applies only to copies manufactured within the United States, or also to copies of a copyrighted work that were manufactured abroad and imported into the United States after a lawful sale overseas. The Court held that the first sale doctrine applies to copies of a copyrighted work lawfully made abroad -- rejecting a geographical limitation on the phrase "lawfully made under this title" in § 109(a).

  "We hold that the “first sale” doctrine applies to copies of a copyrighted work lawfully made abroad."
  — Kirtsaeng v. John Wiley & Sons, Inc., 568 U.S. 519, 525 (2013) (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/2959744/kirtsaeng-v-john-wiley-sons-inc/)

UMG RECORDINGS, INC. V. AUGUSTO: A DISTRIBUTION LABELED A "LICENSE" CAN STILL BE A TRANSFER OF TITLE
In UMG Recordings, Inc. v. Augusto, the Ninth Circuit addressed whether promotional compact discs a record company mailed, unsolicited, to music critics and radio programmers -- marked with a statement describing the discs as the company's property, "licensed" to the recipient, with resale said to be prohibited -- were nonetheless transferred in ownership to the recipients for first-sale purposes, notwithstanding that label. On the record before it, the court found no evidence that any recipient had agreed to the stated license terms, and held that the distributor's transfer of possession -- made without retaining meaningful control over the discs or any knowledge of their status after shipment -- accomplished a transfer of title rather than a license. The court concluded that the distribution of the promotional discs, under those circumstances, effected a sale (a transfer of title) of the discs to the recipients, so that a subsequent sale of those particular discs by someone who acquired them from a recipient did not require the distributor's authorization.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-10]
  "Because the record here is devoid of any indication that the recipients agreed to a license, there is no evidence to support a conclusion that licenses were established under the terms of the promotional statement. Accordingly, we conclude that UMG’s transfer of possession to the recipients, without meaningful control or even knowledge of the status of the CDs after shipment, accomplished a transfer of title."
  — UMG Recordings, Inc. v. Augusto, 628 F.3d 1175 (9th Cir. 2011) (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/182134/umg-recordings-inc-v-augusto/)
  "UMG’s distribution of the promotional CDs under the circumstances effected a sale (transfer of title) of the CDs to the recipients. Further sale of those copies was therefore permissible without UMG’s authorization."
  — UMG Recordings, Inc. v. Augusto, 628 F.3d 1175 (9th Cir. 2011) (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/182134/umg-recordings-inc-v-augusto/)

UMG RECORDINGS, INC. V. AUGUSTO: CALLING AN ARRANGEMENT A "LICENSE" IS A FACTOR, NOT THE DECIDING FACTOR
Separate from the specific facts of the promotional-CD distribution before it, the Ninth Circuit stated a general principle drawn from its own prior software-licensing decisions: in deciding whether an arrangement transferring a copy of a copyrighted work is a sale or a license for first-sale purposes, a party's own labeling of the arrangement as a "license" is a factor a court considers, but that labeling is not, by itself, the deciding factor.

expectedJSON.body: The U.S. Supreme Court has described what the first sale doctrine accomplishes in § 106(3) exhaustion terms: once a copy of a copyrighted work has been lawfully sold, or its ownership otherwise lawfully transferred, the "first sale" is said to have "exhausted" the copyright owner's exclusive distribution right under § 106(3) as to that particular copy, leaving the buyer and subsequent owners of that copy free to dispose of it as they wish. In Kirtsaeng v. John Wiley & Sons, Inc., the Court addressed whether this doctrine applies only to copies manufactured within the United States, or also to copies of a copyrighted work that were manufactured abroad and imported into the United States after a lawful sale overseas. The Court held that the first sale doctrine applies to copies of a copyrighted work lawfully made abroad -- rejecting a geographical limitation on the phrase "lawfully made under this title" in § 109(a).

citations.quote: In copyright jargon, the “first sale” has “exhausted” the copyright owner’s § 106(3) exclusive distribution right.

expectedJSON.body: In UMG Recordings, Inc. v. Augusto, the Ninth Circuit addressed whether promotional compact discs a record company mailed, unsolicited, to music critics and radio programmers -- marked with a statement describing the discs as the company's property, "licensed" to the recipient, with resale said to be prohibited -- were nonetheless transferred in ownership to the recipients for first-sale purposes, notwithstanding that label. On the record before it, the court found no evidence that any recipient had agreed to the stated license terms, and held that the distributor's transfer of possession -- made without retaining meaningful control over the discs or any knowledge of their status after shipment -- accomplished a transfer of title rather than a license. The court concluded that the distribution of the promotional discs, under those circumstances, effected a sale (a transfer of title) of the discs to the recipients, so that a subsequent sale of those particular discs by someone who acquired them from a recipient did not require the distributor's authorization.

citations.quote: Because the record here is devoid of any indication that the recipients agreed to a license, there is no evidence to support a conclusion that licenses were established under the terms of the promotional statement. Accordingly, we conclude that UMG’s transfer of possession to the recipients, without meaningful control or even knowledge of the status of the CDs after shipment, accomplished a transfer of title.

UMG’s distribution of the promotional CDs under the circumstances effected a sale (transfer of title) of the CDs to the recipients. Further sale of those copies was therefore permissible without UMG’s authorization.
